paragraphs: A prototype classifier represents each class through a class-specific reference built from examples. This is attractive for recognizing new classes from little data because it avoids fitting a new classifier each time. The paper asks whether this convenience can be retained without the meta-learning procedure used by prototypical networks.

Simply constructing prototypes from the features of a standard pretrained model does not work as well in the authors’ experiments. They therefore derive a generalization bound to understand how transforming those features could improve classification. The analysis motivates examining normalization methods and the relationship between variation within a class and separation between classes.

Experimentally, L2 normalization and reducing the ratio of within-class variance to between-class variance achieve performance comparable to the alternatives discussed, without meta-learning or training a new classifier. The finding makes feature preparation central to the comparison: the usefulness of a simple prototype classifier depends on how its feature space is organized, not just on the availability of pretrained features.
neurips-2022-a-closer-look-at-prototype-.tldr: Careful feature normalization lets prototype classifiers match the studied alternatives without meta-learning or fitting new classifiers.

paragraphs: Meta-learning concerns how experience across related tasks improves the learning process itself. This paper approaches that question through mechanisms that could plausibly operate in neural circuits. It introduces a rule that estimates gradients for the parameters of an underlying learning algorithm by running that algorithm twice and using a contrastive procedure.

The rule extends the idea of contrastive Hebbian learning to meta-learning. It avoids computing second derivatives and running computations backward through time, both of which pose difficulties for a physical neural implementation. Its updates use information presumed to be available locally at neurons and synapses, making that locality an explicit part of the proposed biological plausibility.

The authors test the rule in two different models: synapses with internal states that retain information shared across tasks, and a two-system architecture in which one network rapidly modulates another. In both cases, it matches or exceeds reference algorithms on benchmark problems. A theoretical analysis of gradient estimation error complements those experiments, supporting the rule as a computational proposal rather than establishing that brains implement it.
neurips-2022-a-contrastive-rule-for-meta.tldr: A contrastive meta-learning rule estimates gradients from two runs while using locally available information and avoiding second derivatives.

paragraphs: Building and evaluating language models increasingly involves combining many curated datasets whose origins are clearly documented. Biomedical datasets are underrepresented in popular data hubs, making this approach harder to apply to biomedical language. BigBio addresses that infrastructure problem through a community library containing more than 126 datasets across 13 task categories and more than 10 languages.

The framework provides programmatic access to both datasets and their metadata, helping researchers assemble collections reproducibly. It also works with platforms for creating prompts and evaluating language models with few examples or no task-specific examples. The paper describes how task schemas are harmonized, how data is audited, and how community contributions are organized.

Two illustrative uses connect this infrastructure to research practice: evaluating biomedical prompts in a zero-shot setting and conducting large-scale learning across multiple tasks. The contribution is a shared foundation for those activities. By making diverse biomedical resources easier to access and combine, BigBio supports systematic data-centered experimentation as an ongoing community effort.
neurips-2022-bigbio-a-framework-for-data.tldr: BigBio organizes biomedical language datasets and metadata into a reproducible community framework for prompting, evaluation, and multitask learning.

paragraphs: Predict+Optimize addresses decisions made through optimization when some required parameters are unknown and must be learned. Branch & Learn provides a framework for constructing the learning component from the algorithm that solves the optimization problem. Its central idea is to use the solver’s existing computational structure as a guide for building the corresponding learning procedure.

The construction applies when a problem has a recursive solution algorithm satisfying the conditions required by the framework. Under those conditions, the authors show how to derive a learning algorithm directly and methodically. Iterative algorithms are also covered by interpreting iteration as a special form of recursion, expanding the scope beyond solvers normally described as recursive.

This connection matters because it supplies a systematic route from a suitable solver to a learning algorithm for decisions with unknown parameters. Extensive experiments report better performance than classical and state-of-the-art approaches. The result combines a conditional construction with empirical support: applicability follows from the solver requirements, while the reported performance advantage comes from the evaluated problems.
neurips-2022-branch-learn-for-recursivel.tldr: Branch & Learn systematically derives learning algorithms from suitable recursive or iterative optimization solvers.

paragraphs: A counterfactual explanation describes how an input could change to receive a desired prediction. CLEAR studies this question for models that predict labels for entire graphs. Comparing the original graph with a generated alternative can help people interpret a model’s decision, but generating such alternatives involves a discrete, irregular space of possible graph changes.

The framework uses a graph variational autoencoder mechanism to support optimization and generalization to unseen graphs. It also addresses a separate concern: whether the generated changes respect causal relationships. Rather than assuming the causal model is already known, CLEAR uses an auxiliary variable to help identify it and promote causality in the generated counterfactuals.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world graphs report advantages over state-of-the-art graph counterfactual methods across different aspects of evaluation. The approach brings generation, generalization, and causal considerations into one framework. Its causal component is described as improving identification and promoting causality, so the stated contribution should not be interpreted as an unconditional guarantee that every generated explanation is causally valid.
neurips-2022-clear-generative-counterfac.tldr: CLEAR generates graph counterfactual explanations with a variational autoencoder and an auxiliary variable that promotes causal consistency.

paragraphs: Deep Model Reassembly explores how to reuse a collection of pretrained networks with different architectures and training sources. The goal is to divide them into building blocks and assemble selected blocks into customized networks. These new networks must meet user-specified hardware resource and performance constraints, making reuse a constrained design problem.

The method jointly partitions the pretrained networks through a cover set optimization. It then forms equivalence sets whose blocks are treated as functionally interchangeable. These sets make it possible to select compatible alternatives when constructing a network. An integer program performs the selection, supported by a training-free proxy that estimates task performance.

The reported reassembled models satisfy the specified constraints while delivering useful predictive performance. On ImageNet, the best reassembled model reaches 78.6% top-1 accuracy without fine-tuning, rising to 83.2% after end-to-end fine-tuning. These results support the practical feasibility of transferring knowledge through network components, including obtaining a functioning model before an additional fine-tuning stage.
neurips-2022-deep-model-reassembly-4de20.tldr: Deep Model Reassembly combines blocks from heterogeneous pretrained networks to build models satisfying resource and performance constraints.

paragraphs: Many biologically plausible learning rules have been proposed, but identifying which rules operate in the brain remains difficult. This paper asks whether changes in neural activity during learning can distinguish supervised learning from reinforcement learning. Its approach depends on the experimenter knowing how neural activity is mapped to behavior.

The distinction comes from credit assignment. In the supervised rules considered, learning uses an internal estimate of how activity affects behavior. An imperfect estimate biases weight updates away from the true gradient direction. The reinforcement-learning rules require no such credit-assignment model and tend to update along the true gradient. The authors derive a metric that uses this difference to distinguish rules through observed activity changes.

Brain-machine interfaces provide a setting where the experimenter can know the activity-to-behavior mapping precisely. Using recurrent neural networks, the authors simulate a cursor-control interface and show that the rules can be distinguished from observations plausibly available in neuroscience experiments. This establishes a discrimination method in simulation under the known-mapping condition.
neurips-2022-distinguishing-learning-rul.tldr: A metric distinguishes supervised and reinforcement learning rules in simulated brain-machine interfaces using observed neural activity changes.

paragraphs: Meta-reinforcement learning trains policies that can quickly adapt to tasks with different rewards or dynamics. That adaptability can remain tied to the particular task distribution used during training. This paper addresses what happens when test tasks come from a shifted distribution, so fast adaptation alone may no longer provide appropriate behavior.

The framework trains a population of meta-policies with different levels of distributional robustness. When presented with a potentially shifted distribution at test time, it selects the policy whose robustness level is most appropriate and uses that policy for fast adaptation. The population therefore provides multiple responses to the possible severity of task distribution shift.

The authors formally show how the framework allows improved regret under distribution shift and demonstrate its effectiveness on simulated robotics problems across a wide range of shifts. The contribution connects robustness selection with meta-learning: preparing policies for different shift levels gives the system a way to adjust its adaptation strategy to the test distribution.
neurips-2022-distributionally-adaptive-m.tldr: A population of differently robust meta-policies enables adaptation to shifted task distributions with formal and simulated support.

paragraphs: The paper treats excessive nonlinearity in neural networks as a source of unstable gradients and weak adversarial robustness. It targets this behavior through curvature, which describes how sharply a model’s response changes. The proposed low-curvature neural networks aim to reduce that sharpness while retaining the predictive performance of standard models.

To make curvature reduction practical, the authors express overall model curvature in terms of the curvatures and slopes of individual layers. They introduce two architectural components for controlling those quantities: centered-softplus, a stable version of the softplus activation, and a batch normalization layer constrained through its Lipschitz behavior. This creates a way to address curvature at the layer level.

Experiments report substantially lower curvature, more stable gradients, and improved adversarial robustness without affecting predictive performance. The approach uses a fraction of the cost of standard adversarial training and can be incorporated into existing architectures. These findings support curvature control as an efficient way to improve the tested networks’ behavior, with robustness gains arising from the proposed architecture and training approach.
neurips-2022-efficient-training-of-low-c.tldr: Controlling layer curvature produces networks with more stable gradients and improved adversarial robustness while preserving predictive performance in experiments.

paragraphs: Proportional fairness is a resource allocation objective used in network flow control, operations research, and economics. It chooses allocation quantities by maximizing the sum of their logarithms. In the packing version studied here, allocation variables are nonnegative and must satisfy positive linear constraints describing the feasible use of resources.

The paper introduces an accelerated first-order method for solving this problem in a distributed way. First-order optimization works with gradient information, while the distributed formulation allows the computation to be organized across participants or components. The authors state that their method improves on previous approaches to the packing proportional fairness problem.

They also develop an algorithm for the dual optimization problem, providing a second route for working with the same allocation structure. Both algorithms are width-independent, a shared property of their computational guarantees. The contribution is thus algorithmic on both sides of the formulation: a faster distributed method for the allocation objective and an accompanying method for its dual.
neurips-2022-fast-algorithms-for-packing.tldr: The paper develops improved width-independent algorithms for packing proportional fairness and its dual.

paragraphs: A point process describes events, and its intensity expresses how their occurrence rate depends on conditions. This paper estimates intensity as a function of covariates while representing uncertainty in a Bayesian way. It introduces an augmented permanental process that places a Gaussian process over covariate space to model prior uncertainty in the square root of intensity.

The key computational result is that a representer theorem holds for this augmented process. This mathematical structure supplies advantages that the authors use to derive a fast estimation algorithm. Its computational cost scales linearly with data size, and it avoids both discretizing the domain and performing Markov Chain Monte Carlo computation.

Evaluations on synthetic and real-world data report better predictive accuracy than state-of-the-art methods and substantially faster computation than a conventional Bayesian method. The contribution links a new probabilistic construction to a tractable inference procedure. It shows how representing uncertainty in event intensity can be combined with computational scaling suited to larger datasets in the tested settings.
neurips-2022-fast-bayesian-estimation-of.tldr: An augmented permanental process enables Bayesian intensity estimation that scales linearly with data size without discretization or MCMC.

paragraphs: Many learning problems require estimating how an expected quantity changes when the parameters of its probability distribution change. For discrete distributions, common gradient estimates can fluctuate heavily between samples. This high variance makes the estimated learning signal less reliable, motivating the paper’s focus on reducing variability in discrete gradient estimation.

The authors introduce a variance reduction technique based on Stein operators for discrete distributions. They use it to construct flexible control variates for the REINFORCE leave-one-out estimator. These control variates adjust the estimator to reduce noise and can be adapted online to minimize variance. Crucially, they do not require additional evaluations of the target function.

On benchmark generative modeling tasks, including binary variational autoencoders, the resulting estimator has substantially lower variance than state-of-the-art alternatives using the same number of function evaluations. That comparison isolates the usefulness of the variance reduction mechanism under an equal evaluation budget. The stated benefit is a more stable gradient estimate without obtaining extra target-function measurements.
neurips-2022-gradient-estimation-with-di.tldr: Discrete Stein operators provide adaptive control variates that reduce gradient variance without extra target-function evaluations.

paragraphs: Inverse problems reconstruct an underlying object from incomplete or transformed measurements. Diffusion models can tackle these problems by modifying their sampling process. Existing solvers discussed here alternate a reverse diffusion step with a projection that enforces agreement with measurements, but this combination can produce suboptimal reconstructions.

The authors analyze the sampling trajectory and identify a geometric problem: those steps can push the trajectory away from the data manifold, allowing errors to accumulate. They introduce an additional correction term inspired by a manifold constraint. It works alongside the existing solvers to keep the iterations close to the manifold while reconstruction proceeds.

The correction requires only a few lines of implementation, yet the paper reports a large performance improvement. The authors support the approach with theoretical and empirical comparisons, including experiments in image inpainting, colorization, and sparse-view computed tomography. The main insight is that measurement consistency must be considered together with the geometry of the generative trajectory when designing diffusion-based reconstruction updates.
neurips-2022-improving-diffusion-models-.tldr: A manifold-inspired correction improves diffusion inverse-problem solvers by keeping reconstruction trajectories close to the data manifold.

paragraphs: Physical simulations can generate data at different levels of fidelity, such as different mesh spacings. Combining cheaper low-fidelity examples with more detailed ones can reduce data generation costs. Infinite Fidelity Coregionalization models fidelity as a continuous quantity, allowing it to capture relationships beyond a fixed collection of discrete simulation levels.

The model represents a high-dimensional simulation output through a low-dimensional latent output multiplied by a basis matrix. A neural ordinary differential equation models the latent output across fidelity and input. Gaussian processes or another differential equation estimate how the bases vary with fidelity, giving both parts of the representation a way to share information across simulation resolutions.

For scalable inference with very large outputs, the method arranges the bases as a tensor and uses a tensor-Gaussian variational approximation. It can interpolate or extrapolate to fidelity levels absent from training data. Results on computational physics benchmarks show advantages for the approach, supporting continuous fidelity modeling as a useful way to improve predictions from simulations of varying resolution.
neurips-2022-infinite-fidelity-coregiona.tldr: Infinite Fidelity Coregionalization learns across continuous simulation fidelities and predicts outputs at fidelity levels unseen during training.

paragraphs: Small decision trees are easy to follow, but deeper trees and ensembles can lose that interpretability as they become more accurate. Shapley values help explain their predictions by assigning contributions to input features. These feature weights provide an explanation that does not require a person to work through the model’s entire tree structure.

Computing Shapley values is generally an exponential-complexity problem. TreeShap made these explanations practical for tree models by solving the computation in polynomial time. As its use expanded, improving the efficiency of that exact computation became valuable. Linear TreeShap is introduced as a more efficient and more straightforward algorithm for the same explanatory purpose.

The new algorithm preserves two properties of TreeShap: its results are exact, and it requires the same amount of memory. The contribution therefore improves the computation of explanations without trading away exactness or increasing memory requirements. Its relevance comes from making a widely used feature-attribution method more efficient as tree-based models become harder to inspect directly.
neurips-2022-linear-tree-shap-983678cb4e.tldr: Linear TreeShap computes exact tree-model Shapley values more efficiently while retaining TreeShap’s memory requirements.

paragraphs: Multi-view subspace clustering combines different descriptions of the same data to find shared groups. A common approach uses self-expression to build affinity representations describing relationships among points. This paper argues that those relationships should also account for the data’s implied manifold structure, which many existing approaches give little attention to.

The proposed model learns topological relationships and incorporates them when merging multiple affinity graphs into one consensus graph. It then imposes a connectivity constraint on that graph so its connected components directly identify the clusters. The final grouping is therefore built into the structure of the learned graph.

This design removes the need for a separate label discretization strategy of the kind used by previous methods. It connects the representation being learned to the clustering result that the method ultimately needs to produce. Experiments on several benchmark datasets demonstrate effective clustering performance compared with state-of-the-art competitors, providing empirical support for incorporating topology and explicit connectivity into the consensus representation.
neurips-2022-multi-view-subspace-cluster.tldr: The method combines multi-view affinity graphs using topology and connectivity constraints so connected components directly yield clusters.

paragraphs: In multi-agent reinforcement learning, value decomposition builds a global assessment from smaller utility functions. Coordination graphs add pairwise payoff functions to represent interactions between agents. However, combining these local functions linearly still limits the global value functions they can express. This paper extends coordination graphs to nonlinear combinations.

Greater expressive power creates a decision problem: selecting the joint action with the highest estimated value becomes harder, and commonly used distributed constraint optimization algorithms no longer apply. The authors study this selection problem for mixing networks with LeakyReLU activations. They propose an enumeration method with a global optimality guarantee.

That enumeration method motivates a more efficient iterative optimization procedure with a local optimality guarantee. The distinction matters because the efficient procedure has a weaker guarantee about the action it finds. Experiments report superior performance on challenging coordination tasks such as MACO, supporting the usefulness of nonlinear value decomposition together with action-selection methods designed for its structure.
neurips-2022-non-linear-coordination-gra.tldr: Nonlinear coordination graphs expand multi-agent value representations and introduce action-selection methods with global or local optimality guarantees.

paragraphs: Boosting combines weak learners into a stronger predictor. This paper studies boosting when predictions are made online, there are multiple possible labels, and learning is agnostic rather than assuming perfectly predictable labels. The combination extends a previously developed approach for online agnostic classification with only two classes.

The central tool is a reduction to online convex optimization. Such a reduction connects the boosting problem to an optimization procedure, allowing an online convex optimizer to serve as a component of the booster. The paper extends this connection to multiclass problems and presents what the authors identify as the first boosting algorithm for online agnostic multiclass classification.

The reduction also supports algorithm construction in three related settings: statistical agnostic, online realizable, and statistical realizable multiclass boosting. Its significance is therefore broader than one algorithm. A common optimization-based construction spans several combinations of learning setting and assumptions, showing how the binary reduction can be extended to a family of multiclass boosting problems.
neurips-2022-online-agnostic-multiclass-.tldr: A reduction to online convex optimization enables online agnostic multiclass boosting and related multiclass boosting constructions.

paragraphs: PAC-Bayesian learning bounds traditionally address a batch setting, where the data is collected before inference or prediction begins. Many learning systems instead receive a stream and must adjust as observations arrive. This paper develops theoretical guarantees suited to that online setting, bringing PAC-Bayesian analysis closer to sequential learning.

The authors prove new bounds using an updated definition of regret, the quantity used to assess performance across an online sequence. They also revisit classical PAC-Bayesian results through a batch-to-online conversion. This extends the reach of those results to dependent data, making the analysis relevant when observations cannot simply be treated as independent.

The guarantees require bounded losses, but those losses may be non-convex. That combination is significant: the theory retains a stated restriction on loss magnitude while allowing a broader shape for the learning objective. The contribution is a set of analytical tools for online learning and dependent observations, providing a basis for further developments rather than an empirical performance claim.
neurips-2022-online-pac-bayes-learning-4.tldr: New PAC-Bayesian bounds cover online learning and dependent data with bounded, potentially non-convex losses.

paragraphs: The paper studies allocation when every recipient must receive a fixed, prespecified fraction of a distribution of items. Alongside those quotas, an allocation should limit envy between recipients. The challenge is to balance allocation efficiency with envy while respecting the required shares, rather than treating complete envy-freeness as the only acceptable outcome.

The authors formulate the problem as a variant of semi-discrete optimal transport. In this formulation, the solution has a compact representation and a simple geometric interpretation. It permits a continuous, optimal trade-off between efficiency and envy, providing a way to vary the balance within a single allocation framework.

The paper also analyzes how these allocation policies can be learned from samples. It establishes a polynomial bound on the number of samples needed to approximate the optimal solution. Numerical results using an existing realistic simulator support the approach for large-scale fair allocation, with blood donation matching as a motivating application. The contribution combines a structured optimization formulation with statistical and simulation-based evidence.
neurips-2022-optimal-efficiency-envy-tra.tldr: An optimal transport formulation continuously balances allocation efficiency and envy while respecting fixed recipient shares.

paragraphs: Multiple-try Metropolis extends Metropolis-Hastings by generating several trial states and choosing a proposal using a weight function. It has shown faster empirical convergence, but the complexity of that proposal mechanism makes its theoretical mixing behavior harder to analyze. This paper studies the issue for discrete state spaces relevant to high-dimensional model selection.

Under a general setting applicable to those problems, the authors prove that multiple-try Metropolis can have a mixing-time bound smaller than the Metropolis-Hastings bound by a factor equal to the number of trials. This is a conditional theoretical improvement in mixing time, tied to the setting covered by the analysis.

The theory also motivates locally balanced weight functions and guides the choice of how many trials to use. Those choices lead to improvements over standard multiple-try Metropolis algorithms. Extensive simulations and real-data applications in Bayesian model selection support the theoretical findings, connecting the mixing analysis to practical decisions about how to construct the sampler.
neurips-2022-rapidly-mixing-multiple-try.tldr: A mixing-time analysis of multiple-try Metropolis motivates improved weighting and trial selection for Bayesian model selection.

paragraphs: Dangerous driving situations are rare and varied, making safety evaluation through ordinary driving extremely demanding. Existing evaluation approaches also differ in simulators, routes, scenarios, and generation methods, complicating comparisons. SafeBench brings these elements into a unified platform so autonomous-driving systems and testing methods can be compared under more consistent conditions.

The platform includes eight safety-critical scenarios following the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration and four scenario generation algorithms, considering ten variations for each scenario. It also implements four driving algorithms based on deep reinforcement learning with four types of input, including camera and bird’s-eye views. This creates a common environment for examining different systems and testing choices.

The authors find that their generated scenarios are more challenging and observe a trade-off between driving-agent performance in benign and safety-critical scenarios. That finding shows why ordinary-condition performance alone is insufficient to characterize the tested agents’ behavior. SafeBench’s contribution is a shared evaluation platform that supports systematic comparison and the development of testing and safe-driving methods.
neurips-2022-safebench-a-benchmarking-pl.tldr: SafeBench unifies autonomous-driving safety evaluation and reveals trade-offs between performance in benign and safety-critical scenarios.

paragraphs: Semi-ViT studies how vision transformers can learn image classification from a mixture of labeled and unlabeled data. Its pipeline begins with unsupervised or self-supervised pretraining, continues with supervised fine-tuning, and finishes with semi-supervised fine-tuning. This sequence combines an initial representation-learning stage with later use of both label sources.

For the final stage, the authors use an exponential-moving-average teacher framework because they find it more stable and accurate than FixMatch for these transformers. They also introduce probabilistic pseudo mixup, which interpolates unlabeled examples and their predicted labels. This supplies regularization, an important concern for vision transformers with weak inductive bias.

Semi-ViT matches or exceeds the studied convolutional-network counterparts in semi-supervised classification and gains accuracy as model size increases. Semi-ViT-Huge reaches 80% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet with only 1% of labels, comparable to Inception-v4 using all ImageNet labels. The result illustrates the reported label efficiency of this training pipeline and its ability to benefit from larger transformer models.
neurips-2022-semi-supervised-vision-tran.tldr: Semi-ViT combines staged training, an EMA teacher, and pseudo mixup to scale semi-supervised vision transformers effectively.

paragraphs: Adversarial robustness is often trained against a single rule defining allowable input perturbations. This paper targets worst-case performance across the union of three threat models: l-infinity, l2, and l1. Covering them together matters because strength against one perturbation model does not by itself address the combined robustness objective.

Existing approaches discussed in the paper use expensive multistep attacks or fine-tune models already robust to a single threat. The authors show that carefully choosing the training objective makes it possible to obtain similar or better worst-case performance across the union using only single-step attacks. This substantially reduces the computational resources needed for training.

They also apply the method specifically to l1 robustness, a setting where prior adversarial training approaches encountered gradient masking. The paper reports the first l1-robust model trained solely with single-step adversaries. A modern collection of attack evaluations is used to better estimate worst-case performance under the considered union, supporting the claimed efficiency and robustness benefits within those threat models.
neurips-2022-toward-efficient-robust-tra.tldr: A carefully chosen objective enables efficient single-step adversarial training against a union of l-infinity, l2, and l1 threats.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must learn from an existing dataset rather than collect new interactions. In a two-player zero-sum Markov game, the goal considered here is learning a Nash equilibrium strategy. This paper asks what assumptions about the dataset make that goal possible, focusing on how adequately the available data covers relevant strategies.

The authors show that single strategy concentration, an assumption used in offline single-agent learning, is insufficient in this game setting. They introduce unilateral concentration and design a pessimism-type algorithm that is provably efficient under that assumption. They also establish that unilateral concentration is necessary for learning a Nash equilibrium strategy in the studied framework.

The same algorithm achieves minimax sample complexity without modification in two settings: datasets satisfying uniform concentration and turn-based Markov games. These results connect a requirement on the available data to both learnability and statistical efficiency. They clarify why an assumption adequate for a single decision-maker does not automatically carry over when learning must account for an opposing player.
neurips-2022-when-are-offline-two-player.tldr: Unilateral concentration characterizes a necessary data condition and supports efficient offline learning of Nash strategies in two-player zero-sum Markov games.
